items.action: Before the railway, transport by boat, sea or river, was the only means of widening markets; navigable rivers extended trading areas along their courses.
Luiz Ferrari de Mordau argued that land transport cost about ten times more than water transport, so river navigation should grow and canals link rivers.

numbers.what: land transport cost relative to water

items.action: Proposal to open a canal linking the Tagus and Sado rivers, between Moita and Setúbal.
The Tagus held major importance as the longest, most easily navigable river and central artery of the Peninsula, until the railway reduced some traffic.
items.period: until the advent of the railway

items.action: Road haulage by lorry finally destroyed river transport along the Tagus completely.
Remaining Tagus traffic is estuary navigation within tidal waters, insignificant beyond 20-30 km upstream of Lisbon.

numbers.what: distance upstream where traffic becomes insignificant

items.action: Figure 1 shows the area that sent its products to Lisbon by the Tagus at the end of the 18th century, with ports such as Santarém, Abrantes and Benavente.
items.place: Lisbon, Santarém, Abrantes, Tancos, Punhete, Barquinha, Benavente

items.action: A 1957 study calculated the total navigable stretches of Portuguese rivers, including 50 km of the Ria de Aveiro.
Only some stretches were permanently navigable by boats over 40 tonnes: Tagus system, Sado and Guadiana shares.

numbers.what: total permanently navigable for boats over 40 t

items.place: Tagus and adjuvant system, Sado, Guadiana

items.action: The Tagus was temporarily navigable for about two months along a longer stretch.
Tradition holds that the Tancos quay, dated to the first half of the 16th century, was built over an earlier, probably Roman, quay.
Santarém was a seaport under the Romans, the Muslims and in the early Portuguese monarchy; in the 13th-14th centuries it traded directly by boat with North Africa and Flanders.
During the Almohad siege of Santarém, Afonso Henriques went up the river with a fleet of crusaders to relieve the city.
According to Severim de Faria, the Templars, defenders of the Tagus line, were first to undertake works to make navigation easier.
After the definitive conquest of the Algarve, the Tagus grew in importance as a communication axis, and Lisbon became capital.
D. Dinis promoted works on the Tagus and its tributary system and founded Salvaterra de Magos and Muge, boosting river navigation.
In the early 15th century Almada and Ribatejo (Montijo) linked Lisbon with the south, with Coina also important; fish from Setúbal and Arrábida came through them.
People and goods from the Alentejo, mainly firewood from Montijo and Canha districts for Lisbon fuel, came via Ribatejo; some fish went on to Santarém and upriver ports.
Salt, fish (dried, salted, smoked or fresh) and cloth were the main goods carried upriver from Lisbon to Santarém, Abrantes and Punhete.
Goods sent downriver to Lisbon included timber, olive oil, wine, hides, honey, wax, iron and river fish (shad, azevias, lampreys).
items.cargo: timber, olive oil, wine, hides, honey, wax, iron, shad, azevias, lampreys

items.action: Santarém was the most important middle Tagus port, followed by Abrantes and Punhete; the author defines the middle Tagus as Abrantes to Sabugueiro, where tide begins.
The 16th century saw a surge in Tagus navigation, with D. Manuel I's works including the imposing Tancos quay.
The king travelled by boat between the Royal Palace of Almeirim and Lisbon (Paço de Xabregas or Paço da Ribeira).
A 1552 count listed river boats at Lisbon and Tagus ports, with Abrantes holding 180, split between regular service and fishing.
items.conditions: author notes the figures are probably exaggerated

numbers.what: river boats in Lisbon and Tagus ports

items.action: In 1552 Tancos had 100 boats, Punhete with Asseiceira and Carvoeira 120, and Santarém 100, the main middle Tagus ports.
Large quantities of melons from the Santarém and Abrantes lezírias were carried to Lisbon as a new item; wine arrived by river, named after loading ports.
Four barcas came from Muge to Lisbon two to three times a week, and likewise from Azambuja.
Three barcas and batéis came from Vila Nova da Rainha to Lisbon two to three times a week.
items.place: Vila Nova da Rainha to Lisbon

items.action: Four barcas came from Benavente to Lisbon three to four times a week.
Brandão gives data only for the lower Tagus, probably because middle and upper river voyages were more irregular owing to various constraints.
Table of boats serving Lisbon by port lists Sacavém, Alhandra and Lisbon and surroundings, totalling 1490 boats and batéis serving Lisbon.
items.boat: barco de Sacavém; boats and batéis

numbers.what: total boats and batéis serving Lisbon

items.action: Boats carried firewood, wheat and straw, plus people and other goods, on weekly runs.
River traffic above Abrantes was of little importance before the Philippine period; Punhete and Abrantes were the upstream ports named in the 15th century, Santarém further downstream.
Abrantes is the furthest upstream port named in the 1552 Lisbon statistics.
Philip II promoted major works to improve Tagus navigation, entrusting study and execution to engineer Joan Baustista Antonelli, removing obstacles between Lisbon and Alcántara.

In the mid-19th century Portuguese boats, mostly from Rossio de Abrantes, Pego and Alvega, carried Alcántara ore to Lisbon in convoys of at least ten boats so crews could help each other with towing at rapids.
items.conditions: rapids; some boats lost in disasters
items.who: tripulações do Rossio de Abrantes, Pego, Alvega

items.action: Towpaths (sirgadouros) were built at the hardest river points and some rocks removed, allowing Estremoz marble to be shipped by river to the Escorial.
Larger boats could not navigate in dry season, even at Abrantes; in summer timber and cork went by raft to Salvaterra de Magos or Valada, then by boat to Lisbon.
items.place: Salvaterra de Magos, Valada, Abrantes, Lisboa

items.action: Antonelli died in 1588; successors including Carduchi and Martelli published the Corografia del Rio Tajo (1641), the first survey with a plan of the Tagus from Toledo to Lisbon.
Table of Tagus port boats in 1620 shows Abrantes (Rossio) as the main river port, with more boats than Santarém, followed by Tancos and Punhete; Barquinha not yet mentioned.
items.place: Abrantes, Santarém, Tancos, Punhete, Muge, Salvaterra, Benavente, Chamusca, Vila

items.action: Wars of the Restoration set back Tagus transport, as relations with Spain disappeared or greatly declined.
Spanish technicians carried out reconnaissance studies of the Tagus to improve links between Extremadura, Castile and the Atlantic.
items.conditions: political upheavals undermined the Lisbon-interior link

items.action: A Tagus navigation plan by Carlos Simon Pontero appeared, and Brigadier Cabanes drew up a steam navigation project from Aranjuez to Lisbon, requesting licences from both governments.
items.who: D. Carlos Simon Pontero; D. Francisco Xavier Cabanes

items.action: Treaty signed in Lisbon by Ferdinand VII and Miguel I legalised the Aranjuez-Lisbon navigation project.
Architect Augustin Martin made the Aranjuez-Lisbon voyage, taking 31 days to Alcántara and 9 more to Lisbon, and 138 days in total on the return.
Manuel Bermudes de Castro, heir of the concessionaires, renewed the contract, provoking protests in the Portuguese press.
A writer argues a Tagus navigation company would not endanger Portugal's independence, with half the sailors Portuguese and a third of shares reserved for Portuguese investors.

numbers.what: share of sailors who would be Portuguese
share of shares reserved for Portuguese capitalists

items.action: Ayres de Sá Nogueira requested a 40-year concession for Tagus navigation up to the frontier; the reply says extending navigation to Toledo would be more useful.
Marble from Estremoz bound for the Escorial was carried by boat up the Tagus as far as Toledo despite difficulties.
Until the late 19th century some improvements were made to regularise the Tagus and ease navigation; many other proposed works were never carried out.
By the end of the 19th century the Portuguese Tagus had masonry towing-path walls, though dams and dikes were still needed.
Spanish engineer Filipe de Mora published a study projecting canalisation of the Manzanares, Jarama and Tagus for 300 t boats between Madrid and Lisboa.
Railways competed with river navigation on several stretches but never proved superior; they won outright only upriver of Abrantes and near Entroncamento, ruining Vila Nova da Barquinha and Moita.
items.place: Abrantes, Entroncamento, Vila Nova da Barquinha, Moita

items.action: After the Second World War boats left Tagus ports, first in the middle course and later the lower course, as road transport outcompeted river navigation.
Boatmen leaving upriver ports moved their boats to work on the lower Tagus; others sold boats and became lorry operators, merchants or retirees.
items.who: barqueiros from Abrantes, Rio de Moinhos, Constância, Chamusca

items.action: Many mariners from Vila Nova da Barquinha and Moita took jobs at the railway company in Entroncamento, leaving the river.
items.place: Vila Nova da Barquinha, Moita, Entroncamento

items.action: Ruined warehouses, guesthouses and inns at Barquinha, Constância and Rossio still show the riverside life once tied to river traffic.
Balbi's statistics list boats and crew at Tagus ports: Barquinha, Porto de Tancos, Abrantes, Constância, Paio de Pele, Tancos and Atalaia.
items.place: Barquinha, Tancos, Abrantes, Constância, Paio de Pele, Atalaia

items.action: Constância, Paio de Pele and Rio de Moinhos had mostly fishermen and seafolk, with few farm workers.

numbers.what: Paio de Pele fishermen and seafolk
Rio de Moinhos fishermen and seafolk

items.place: Constância, Paio de Pele, Rio de Moinhos

items.action: Constância had a growing population, mostly working in navigation; farm and grape-harvest labour came from nearby villages, Vila de Rei and Cardigos.
Tancos, then an important port, had a workforce dominated by sailors and boat owners, per the 1763 tax record studied by Jorge Borges de Macedo.
Tancos suffered heavy damage in the French invasions and many inhabitants emigrated to Lisbon; Abrantes and Barquinha gained its traffic, including Alentejo wheat.
The author introduces summaries of his 1969-1970 interviews in former river ports, beginning with Pedro Maria Duarte, a retired boat builder at Rossio.
A boatbuilder, whose father and grandfather also built boats at Barreiras do Tejo, was the last to stop working in the Abrantes area; some of his boats still work around Lisbon.
His grandfather had carried ore from Alcántara by boat; the railway stopped upstream traffic beyond Alvega.
The railway initially raised the importance of the river port of Rossio de Abrantes, which around 1920 had many large boats; trucks then began its decline.
River traffic at Rossio revived somewhat during the Second World War, but ended completely by the early 1950s.
Boat trips from Rossio to Lisbon took about 4 days on average, ranging from 2 to 5 days; the return varied from 2 to 30 days.
items.conditions: downstream by sail or oar; return by sail and pole
items.gear: sail, oars downstream; sail and pole upstream

items.action: José da Silva, a former boat businessman, had a 60 t boat built at Constância by the Zêzere in 1945 and sold it to Alcochete two years before the interview.
His last freight of timber from Constância to Lisbon was 23 years earlier; afterwards he carried fertilisers and sulphates from CUF Barreiro to Santarém for onward rail transport.
items.conditions: goods continued by train from Santarém

items.action: He later worked the Lisbon markets, carrying wine from Sabugueiro, Cartaxo, Salvaterra and Vala do Carregado to Lisbon and Cacilhas (Ginjal); he sold his boat in 1958 and retired.
items.place: Sabugueiro; Cartaxo; Salvaterra; Vala do Carregado; Lisboa; Cacilhas

items.action: Until the late 1950s boats up to 30 t left Rossio de Abrantes with cork and timber for Lisbon.
Constância to Lisbon could take a day and a half; the round trip averaged 15 days. Floods could hold boats up to 18 days at Sabugueiro, where tidal waters begin.
items.conditions: floods; tidal waters start at Sabugueiro

items.action: Around 1930 Constância had about 30 boats of 25-40 t and as many of 10-12 t; Rossio had more; Barquinha, Amoreira and Rio de Moinhos about 10 each.

numbers.what: boats at Barquinha, Amoreira, Rio de Moinhos each

items.place: Constância; Rossio; Barquinha; Amoreira; Rio de Moinhos

items.action: In the 1930s seamen of Barquinha and Moita moved to the railway; C.P. bought some boats at Vila Nova da Barquinha, and José da Silva bought one there.
items.who: seamen of Barquinha and Moita; C. P.

items.action: Timber rafts went from Praia do Ribatejo to Valada or Salvaterra until 1950.
In José da Silva's childhood the Zêzere was navigable for 15 t boats up to Barca Nova.

Until the 1930s Constância was a town of seafarers and traders who bought goods in the Beiras, Alentejo and Alta Estremadura to sell in Lisbon; ground-floor shops and taverns hosted card and chinquilho games.
Floods seldom caused great damage on Rua Grande; in summer the Tejo was so low that a boat with a 20 m mast showed no mast.
Of 15 Constância boatmen recalled, 4 opened taverns, 1 went to the lower Tejo and returned, 1 became a river contractor, 1 farmed, and 8 took boats to Lisbon and worked for others.
items.place: Constância; baixo Tejo; Lisboa; Castanheira do Ribatejo

items.action: Manuel da Fonseca and his brother left boating for the railways 47 years earlier; their father, who owned 2 upstream boats, sold the last one 40 years ago.
Many Barquinha boat owners lived in Moita village; Barquinha was always seen as dead because Entroncamento took its trade and fair.
José Bragança, ferry concessionaire at Vila Nova da Barquinha, said Barquinha was the first port to die; the last boat, Alfredo Condesso's, lasted until the late 1930s.
Bartolomeu Pereira da Silva moved to the lower Tejo and does river works contracting; his few fragatas mainly carry building materials, since freights to Salvaterra or Benavente are scarce.

numbers.what: years since moving to lower Tejo

items.action: Study limited to the period before railways and cars, expecting river (Tagus) and sea transport to distort Von Thünen's circular land-use model around Lisbon.
Fig. 5 maps land-use organisation around Lisbon before the railway, showing how each product's tolerance for transport cost shaped production for the Lisbon market.
Glass factories were forbidden within a set distance of Lisbon.

numbers.what: limit within which glass factories could not exist

items.action: Lisbon's jurisdiction for supplying itself with meat (1564) and wheat (1574) extended to a set limit, running along the river to Abrantes.
In 1705 a wider limit applied to Lisbon's supply of meat, firewood and other provisions.
Évora had its own smaller zones of market gardens, firewood, vines, cereal and cork-oak woodland, showing similar systems within each territory.
Around Lisbon's built-up area lay a ring of market gardens, then vineyards for the city's immediate wine consumption.
Wine from Caparica, Barreiro, Alhos Vedros and Seixal was the first large-scale activity on the south bank.
Milk and fresh dairy products (butter, fresh cheese) were produced close to the city for immediate consumption.
Wine from Lisbon's own district had market advantages: priority in sale and lower taxes, though its price was among the highest.
Firewood was essential for households and industries; being bulky and cheap, it needed low transport costs, so production lay near the market.
A long firewood-producing belt ran along the left bank to Benavente and inland near Vendas Novas, with no matching belt to the north.
items.place: left bank of the Tagus; Benavente; Vendas Novas

items.action: Firewood supply areas on Lisbon's right bank were destroyed; Monsanto was totally deforested by accelerated consumption and several lime kilns.
Lisbon's council consulted the king on regulating coal and firewood supply, naming the main supplying districts and towns, including Castanheira do Ribatejo.
items.place: Banda d'Além, Ribatejo, Almada, Aldeia Gallega, Benavente, Samora, Canha, Castan

items.action: Lime-kiln owners complained about the price of brushwood; the council asked the king to order nearby councils to make bundles per old regulations.
items.place: Almada, Alhos Vedros, Aldeia Galega, Alcochete

items.action: The king gave orders to judges of several south-bank towns in similar circumstances concerning supply.
items.place: Aldeia Galega, Almada, Palmela, Moita, Alcochete

items.action: Pine poles were being fetched from woods near Vendas Novas, far from the Tagus, and cartage cost more than the wood once did.
Early in the 17th century, Lisbon's supply area reportedly extended little beyond Alcochete.
The king repeatedly legislated to manage recurring firewood supply crises to Lisbon; crises are noted in 1456, 1562, 1685 and 1726.
Heath scrub on the poor sandy charneca was kept productive for firewood and charcoal, with the king caring for it as the most profitable use for the nation.
items.place: charneca, south bank of the Tagus
items.who: the king; Luiz Mendes de Vasconcellos (author)

items.action: In the 19th century other products became more profitable than scrub, and vineyards gradually replaced it in the Poceirão-Taipadas-Canha area.
When transporting firewood stopped paying, it was made into charcoal; charcoal-burning areas on the periphery moved closer to the river and stopped exporting firewood to Lisbon.
Distant areas with good sea access supplied charcoal to Lisbon: the coast from Feira to Buarcos, the Algarve and the Alentejo coast.
items.place: Feira to Buarcos coast, Algarve, Alentejo coast to Lisbon

items.action: Even more distant areas shipped ash, a more processed, cheaper-to-transport product made from firewood; ash from the Alentejo reached Lisbon through Tagus ports.
The king more than once banned glass furnaces within seven leagues of Lisbon, measures aimed mainly at the south bank.
items.place: within seven leagues of Lisbon, mainly Outra Banda

items.action: Soap works in the 18th century were mostly along the Tagus, using ash arriving by river, while others inland used local raw material.
Tile and brick kilns stood from Almada to Almeirim on the south bank and from Azambuja to Lisbon on the north, mostly by the river, later using south-bank firewood.
items.conditions: need for large amounts of fuel
items.place: Almada to Almeirim; Azambuja to Lisbon

items.action: Lime kilns on the north side, where suitable limestone exists, sent lime to Lisbon through the nearest river ports.
items.place: north bank of the Tagus to Lisbon

items.action: Lime kilns at Alenquer, Ota, Atouguia das Cabras and Portela shipped lime to Lisbon via the port of Vila Nova da Rainha.
items.place: Vila Nova da Rainha, upstream of Alverca

items.action: Lime from Aveiras went out through Virtudes; from Pontével and Cartaxo through Vale da Pedra; from Almoster through Porto de Muge.
items.place: Virtudes, Vale da Pedra, Porto de Muge

items.action: Far from the Tagus and other river routes (Sado, Guadiana), scrub had no use beyond sparse goat grazing and beekeeping; Silveira in 1789 described Alentejo heaths.
Land near the Tagus once held cork oaks that gave owners good income; they sold the trees to charcoal makers and left sterile goat pasture.
items.conditions: owners wanted a single year's returns from many years

items.action: Lisbon's outskirts wines could compete with Torres Vedras and Tagus Lezírias supply only through privileges and better quality; the Lezírias were the main supply area.
items.place: Lisbon, Torres Vedras, Lezírias do Tejo

items.action: Wines from distant Alentejo and Douro could compete in Lisbon only through high quality, and sources always praise them.
Lisbon's municipal council consulted the king about vine growers of Valada, Santarém, Golegã, Torres Vedras, Azeitão and Lisbon, noting field vines were tended every four years.

numbers.what: years between vine tending in the fields

items.place: Campos de Valada, Santarém, Golegã, Torres Vedras, Azeitão, Lisbon

items.action: When wine came from too far and quality could not cover freight, it was turned into brandy to cut mass and cargo cost.
items.conditions: surplus Douro wine that could not be exported
items.place: Douro, Madeira, S. Miguel, Pico, Faial, Lisbon

items.action: Timber near Lisbon was exhausted early, so from the monarchy's start new forests were sown in areas with easy drainage of products.
Timber was brought to Lisbon by sea from Alfeizerão.
Timber kept coming from Alfeizerão-Alcobaça, and also from Leiria and Torres Vedras overland, probably mixed road and river transport.
items.conditions: overland for Leiria and Torres Vedras

items.action: Timber from the Zêzere basin reached the Tagus by floating or ox carts, then was loaded onto rafts or boats; the area drove river transport.
items.conditions: river floating conditions on the Zêzere
items.period: until the end of the first half of the 2

items.action: Leiria and Zêzere-middle Tagus forests were well placed, so Lisbon never had serious timber shortages, unlike many European cities.
England imported timber from Scandinavia, Russia and North America because its oak forests lay too far from coast or waterways.

numbers.what: usual limit of land transport for timber

items.action: Wheat for Lisbon's market stays profitable over longer distances; it grows near Lisbon and in the Ribatejo lezírias, which supply earliest thanks to higher yields.
Alentejo has the large extensive cereal production, more intensive near local centres, good river or sea access and fertile soils.
Olive growing spread as monoculture far from Lisbon because olive oil is cheap to transport relative to its value, though much output was sent to Lisbon.
items.conditions: transport cost low relative to value

items.action: Wine warehouses and wine-processing installations stayed beside Tagus river ports, some still in places unsuited to present transport, such as Ginjal at Cacilhas and Poço do Bispo.
items.place: Vala do Carregado, Cacilhas (Ginjal), Poço do Bispo, Sacavém, Rossio de Abrantes

items.action: Lisbon's municipal council complained to the king that large wine losses and frauds occurred in warehouses, especially foreigners', between Cacilhas and Trafaria.
Foreigners stored wine in warehouses at the entrance of the Trancão river at Sacavém, ready for shipment, as the parish priest reported.
A soap factory still operates at Rossio de Abrantes, probably linked to the origin of its raw materials, ash and vegetable fats.
Timber received first treatment at the felling site: felled trees were cleaned and trunks sorted by size, reducing mass and transport cost before shipping.
items.conditions: transport cheap but processing still worthwhile

items.action: Trunks were carried to the Tagus by ox carts, or floated down the Zêzere, then embarked at river points for Lisbon.
Embarkation points on the Tagus became sites of timber industry and trade, linking pine forests of Alto Ribatejo and Beira Baixa to Lisbon, the main market and export centre.
items.place: Abrantes (Alferrarede, port Barreiras do Tejo), Rio de Moinhos, Praia do Ribatej

items.action: Amoreira was an important timber embarkation point for Lisbon but developed no related industry; Rio de Moinhos dominated the timber trade, and nearby Montalvo got a sawmill.
Lisbon's timber industry first located according to river transport; timber yards and sawmills still line the port at Xabregas, Cais do Tojo, Poço do Bispo and Alcântara.
items.place: Lisbon: Xabregas, Cais do Tojo, Poço do Bispo, Alcântara

items.action: Queen Elizabeth I of England banned ironworkers from using trees over 30 cm in diameter within 22 km of the sea, cited as a precedent.
Specialised timber men guided floating logs down the Zêzere from the banks using a pole tipped with a curved iron hook, until the Castelo de Bode dam was built.
items.period: until the Castelo de Bode dam

items.action: In the rainy season boats went up the Zêzere as far as Barca Nova to load brushwood bundles (fachina).
Timber was taken from the riverbed at a large sandbank below the confluence, loaded on rafts to Valada or Salvaterra, then carried by boat to Lisbon.
items.place: sandbank below Zêzere confluence, Valada, Salvaterra, Lisbon

items.action: A small sawmill industry using hand saws developed at Praia do Ribatejo; steam saws were later introduced and the industry expanded.
Around 1900 a relative of the first industrialist set up a second sawmill; both lasted to the present day of the text.
A sawmill from Abrantes opened a branch at Praia do Ribatejo, which lasted until the end of the first quarter of the 20th century.
Railways served the sawmills for some products, but rafts and boats stayed in use until the Second World War, after which lorries ended river traffic.
items.place: Praia do Ribatejo, Rio de Moinhos

items.action: Rio de Moinhos timber merchants hauled wood by ox cart to the Tagus, then shipped it to Lisbon by boat and raft.
items.place: Rio de Moinhos to Tagus to Lisbon
items.who: timber merchants of Rio de Moinhos

items.action: A fine quay far from the village, built early in the century, served almost solely for timber export; a plaque dates it to 28-11-1903.
Each Rio de Moinhos sawmill owned boats and organised rafts to carry timber downriver; the largest also had a depot at Valada receiving rafted timber for boats to Lisbon.

numbers.what: sawmills built at Rio de Moinhos

items.action: The largest firm also had a depot at Praia do Ribatejo by the Zêzere-Tagus confluence, abandoned a little over twenty years before the text.
The two surviving Rio de Moinhos sawmills were founded late in the 19th century by two partners from an Alferrarede sawmill, exploiting the ox cart to boat transfer point.
During the Second World War the firm Zeferino Álvaro Pereira & Herdeiros built a new boat replacing an identical one; it made two Lisbon trips and was sold to Lisbon shipowners.
items.conditions: firm already owned a producer-gas lorry

items.action: The firm now works only with lorries, from pine woods to factory and to markets, with main clients at Xabregas, Moscavide and Alcântara along Lisbon harbour.
Cork industry is discussed through two examples tied to river transport, Rossio ao Sul do Tejo and Chamusca; large-scale cork industrialisation coincided with the railway.
items.place: Rossio ao Sul do Tejo, Chamusca

items.action: Most cork reached Rossio de Abrantes by rail, then went by boat, more rarely by raft, to the Lisbon area.
items.place: Rossio de Abrantes to Lisbon area

items.action: Cork from Alto Alentejo reached Rossio de Abrantes by rail from Ponte de Sor or on mule carts, often owned by Algarvians who came up for the cork harvest.
items.place: Rossio de Abrantes; Ponte de Sor

items.action: Railway ended boat traffic upstream of Abrantes (Alvega) but increased goods reaching Rossio from the Alentejo, notably cork, coal and cereals, per a former boat builder.
items.who: antigo construtor de barcos de rio acima, do Rossio

items.action: Road transport finally destroyed the remaining river and rail-linked traffic at Rossio about twenty years before the text was written.
Cork was taken to riverside warehouses in summer and shipped by boat in winter; summer rafts, mainly used for timber, carried much less cork. It left raw.
items.conditions: summer by warehouse, winter by boat

items.action: In the 19th century an English firm with a depot at Rossio founded a small plant for first processing of cork into planks.
A small cork industry boom early in the 20th century, also at Ponte de Sor, made transport to Lisbon cheaper.
items.place: Rossio de Abrantes; Ponte de Sor

items.action: Cork industry grew most about thirty years earlier; a dozen factories now make planks, stoppers, panels and agglomerates, employing roughly ten to just over fifty workers each.
Rossio's cork industry boom was driven largely by Spanish capital and technicians from Catalonia and San Vicente de Alcántara; local river-trade capital also converted into it.
items.who: Spanish investors and technicians; local capitalists

items.action: Chamusca was a smaller cork shipping port with a narrower catchment, lacking a railway; cork came to the river by ox or mule carts.
Chamusca had a specialised cork wharf where the product was stored; trade was dominated by English and Americans. River traffic ended with cars after the Second World War.
Chamusca's cork industry predates 1876; the 1890 survey found one small unit with 3 workers. A factory by the cork port stopped working decades ago.
Rossio was the upper limit for boats of 50-70 t, with upstream navigation much harder, so it became an intense wholesale centre supplying the Alentejo and Beira Baixa muleteers.
Boats returning upriver from Lisbon carried salt, salted fish, other food and manufactures to Rossio; wine came mainly from Almeirim and Chamusca.
items.cargo: salt, salted fish (sardine, tuna, dogfish), food, manufactures, wine
items.place: Lisboa; Rossio de Abrantes; Almeirim; Chamusca

items.action: Rossio redistributed goods to local trade and to muleteers from the Alentejo and Beira, who brought back olive oil, potatoes, cheese and other goods.
items.who: almocreves do Alentejo e da Beira

items.action: The railway reduced and nearly ended the flow of muleteers from the Beiras and Alentejo, though Rossio kept its wholesale role.
Liquid fuel was carried by barge from Lisbon to Abrantes; at the Rossio quay, pumps and piping moved it from boats into depots beside the railway station.
items.conditions: depots were built next to the railway station

items.action: Many wholesalers of groceries, wine and salt left Rossio; new truck-based wholesalers set up along main roads instead of at the quay.
items.conditions: abandoned warehouses beside the old quay remain

items.action: Main river ports of the intermediate Tagus are spaced at similar distances, excluding the stretch above Abrantes and below Azambuja; the groups listed include Constância, Tancos, Barquinha-Chamusca, Santarém, Sabugueiro, Valada and Salvaterra.
items.conditions: Sabugueiro, Valada and Salvaterra lie in tidal waters
items.location: Localização, sítio e morfologia das aglomerações portuárias

items.action: Port location is determined mainly by the areas the port serves; the 1807 road map shows each port commanded the road network converging on it.
items.conditions: some authors link ports to old fords used by armies
items.location: Localização, sítio e morfologia das aglomerações portuárias

items.action: Local site factors for ports: a ford, a raised spot near the bed protecting from floods and enemies, a confluence of two navigable rivers, or deeper water allowing quays.
items.location: Localização, sítio e morfologia das aglomerações portuárias

items.action: Abrantes sits on a defensive hilltop away from the river, linked to its quay at Barreiras do Tejo by a steep direct path, the caminho da barca.
items.conditions: quay on the shallow side; water reaches it only in the wet season, far from the water in summer

items.action: Because a quay was feasible only on the left bank, Rossio de Abrantes developed as the long-distance port serving Abrantes and handling goods to and from the Alentejo.
items.cargo: goods from and to the Alentejo

items.action: Rossio and Abrantes were connected by a rudimentary bridge in summer and by small boats between Rossio and Barreiras do Tejo the rest of the year.
Boats carried goods to Lisbon, mostly from the Alentejo: wheat before the railway, then cork as its trade grew.
Timber from areas north of the Tagus was the main export by volume from Abrantes, but mostly travelled on rafts rather than boats.
Abrantes' quay area sits in the seasonal flood bed, while the town lies on the flat terrace above; an old ruined bridge lies upstream of the late-19th-century bridge.
Punhete (Constância) was built on the right bank at the confluence with the Zêzere, where the Tagus is deepest, with its civic centre by the quay in the flood bed.
items.conditions: port areas duplicated; town spreads along the slopes of the Tagus and Zêzere

items.action: Timber from the north floated down the Zêzere and was collected on a beach just downstream of the confluence with the Tejo.
Praia do Ribatejo developed as a secondary port specialised in exporting timber, sent down the Tejo by boats and especially rafts, mainly in summer.
items.conditions: summer, when water was too shallow to load boats

items.action: A small quay opposite Praia do Ribatejo exported coal from the Alentejo but was never important and produced no settlement.
In the early 19th century Tancos's port functions were split between Abrantes and Barquinha; Punhete probably also benefited from Tancos's decline.
Heavy silting left Vila Nova da Barquinha's original quay far from the river, so landing places linked to the town by perpendicular roads had to be created.
items.place: Vila Nova da Barquinha (porto do Dr. Pombeiro, porto da Barca, porto da Fábrica

items.action: Santarém's important port lay on the same bank as the city, giving rise to the Ribeira de Santarém suburb in the river's flood bed.
At Valada, where the Tejo becomes tidal, timber rafted down in summer was transshipped to boats that carried it to Lisboa.
Valada was an important stopping point on river traffic, so much that the king had a palace there.
Dikes were built to protect Valada from floods; the present embankment is recent but probably follows earlier ones.
Salvaterra de Magos and Benavente were tidal river ports; Salvaterra on an improved small tributary, Benavente by the Sorraia and the artificial Vala Nova canal.
items.place: Salvaterra de Magos, Benavente, Sorraia, Vala Nova

items.action: Ports near the Tejo mouth, such as Vila Franca, Alhandra, Póvoa de Santa Iria and Sacavém, behave more like sea ports in a gentle gulf.
items.place: Vila Franca, Alhandra, Póvoa de Santa Iria, Sacavém, south bank ports

items.action: Amoreira and Rio de Moinhos have linear layouts perpendicular to a distant river; their quays only export raw materials, namely timber, and never grew into settlements.
Abrantes's Rossio is organised around a quay running along the river, with three perpendicular streets serving two urban nuclei linked by Rua Direita.
Rossio de Abrantes grew along a riverside street parallel to the Tagus, with a series of squares at the centre of each urban nucleus, between the quays and the interior.
Main buildings of three or four floors, plus commerce especially upstream and along Rua Direita, were built around the squares mostly in the previous century.
Warehouses tied to river traffic stood beside the quay and on transverse streets; some survive today in ruins of varying decay.
A road bridge was built downstream and the settlement extended slightly in that direction.
Railway construction created a suburb (Carvalhal) beside the station, which later merged with the Rossio as motor traffic grew.
Banks, cafés, clothes shops and the main pension moved to the national road linking Ponte de Sor, Abrantes and Lisbon, reversing the earlier habit of locating near the station.
A new road to Gavião-Nisa-Portalegre was built and road traffic grew as river traffic declined, so the Rossio centre moved up toward the national road.
Rossio de Abrantes is presented as a typical Tagus port settlement on flat ground, shaped by river activities, later pulled toward station and highways.
At Samora Correia on the Sorraia, the motor car replaced the boat for local transport, so urban change was simpler, without a railway.
Samora Correia's life slid inland parallel to the river; it is now being drawn toward the Porto Alto crossroads where two national roads meet.
Ports on steep slopes such as Constância, Tancos and Vila Nova da Barquinha show a similar pattern: quayside square, with a parallel road above attracting commerce and services.
items.place: Constância, Tancos, Vila Nova da Barquinha

items.action: Constância sits where two rivers meet on uneven ground; its riverside square is more important and the parallel road runs one way, away from the confluence.
The French summary says Tagus navigation survived railway competition but succumbed to motor transport; it notes the state of navigable Portuguese rivers in 1957.
Boats of 50 to 60 tonnes had long sailed the Tagus up to Abrantes, the main economic axis supporting Lisbon's growth.
In the Middle Ages the port of Santarém kept direct maritime links with North Africa and central Europe.
Abrantes organised foreign trade for much of the Beira and Upper Alentejo.
Goods carried upriver on the Tagus were mainly food, especially salt and fish, and manufactured products.
Farm, livestock and forest products travelled down the Tagus to Lisbon; a 17th-century author's map shows the regions that shipped goods this way.
Philippe II made a major effort to create river links between Lisbon and central Iberia (Aranjuez), after having the river's course studied.
Works removed reefs, built towpaths and improved quays, making navigation possible from Abrantes to the frontier.
Until the railway arrived, the Spanish town of Alcantara exported its ores down the Tagus to Lisbon.
The railway ended all navigation upstream of Abrantes and nearly killed the port of Vila Nova da Barquinha, near a major rail junction.
items.place: upstream of Abrantes, Vila Nova da Barquinha

items.action: The railway company offered boatmen jobs and advantages, sometimes buying their boats.
Lorries, mainly since the last war, finished river navigation, now limited to the estuary.
Boatmen's fates differed: some moved to the estuary with their boats, some turned to trade or farming at home, some drive lorries.
Transport cost distance mainly shaped land use around Lisbon, as in Von Thünen's model: market gardens, quality wine, firewood, charcoal, cheap wine and wheat in rings.

numbers.what: distance of cheap wine and wheat zone from Lisbon

items.action: Timber from interior regions was floated down the Zêzere, then rafted on the Tagus to the tidal limit, where boats carried it to Lisbon.
items.conditions: to the limit of the tide

items.action: Timber from the western coast reached Lisbon by sea, lowering transport costs.
Goods from farthest away bore transport costs best: ashes, olive oil, meat and cheese.
Wheat from nearby Tagus areas reached Lisbon at harvest time; wheat from distant Alentejo arrived later.
Wholesale wine merchants' warehouses have for centuries stood on the south shore opposite Lisbon and in ports just upstream.
items.place: south bank of Tagus estuary, upstream ports

items.action: Some industries and wholesalers once on Lisbon's riverfront moved to the city's northern edge, following rail and lorry transport.
Sawmills at Rio de Moinhos stand on a former timber-loading port for Lisbon; those at Praia do Ribatejo are where floated logs from the Zêzere stopped.
items.place: Rio de Moinhos, Praia do Ribatejo

items.action: The cork industry settled at Rossio de Abrantes and Chamusca, river ports where cork was the main export.
Rossio de Abrantes became a leading wholesale grocery centre thanks to its port, which outlasted the railway; road traffic now replaces it.
Before cars, customers, mainly muleteers, came to the wholesaler; now wholesalers visit clients from Beira to Alentejo.
items.place: Rossio de Abrantes, Beira to Alentejo

items.action: The last chapter presents the situation, site and plan of Tagus ports: Rossio de Abrantes-Barreiras do Tejo, Constância-Praia do Ribatejo, and Chamusca.
items.place: Rossio de Abrantes, Barreiras do Tejo, Constância, Praia do Ribatejo, Chamusca

items.action: Port town plans show life shaped by the main activity; services clustered in streets parallel to the river and on riverside squares.
Tagus was navigable by craft of limited tonnage and served as the main economic axis, linking inland harbours, Lisbon and foreign countries; Santarém and Abrantes were key trading ports.
items.boat: craft up to 50 to 60 tons as far as Abrantes

numbers.what: maximum craft tonnage as far as Abrantes

items.action: Salt, fish and manufactured goods were carried up the Tagus; agricultural, livestock and forest products went downstream to Lisbon.
items.cargo: salt, fish, manufactured products upstream; agricultural, livestock and forest p

items.action: Philip II ordered the river studied and works done (clearing obstacles, towing paths, better piers) to make it navigable from Abrantes to the frontier, linking Lisbon with Aranjuez.
Before railways, the Spanish town of Alcantara exported its ore down the Tagus via Lisbon.
Railways ended all navigation upstream of Abrantes and nearly killed Vila Nova da Barquinha's port; the railway company gave boat owners jobs and advantages, sometimes buying their boats.
items.conditions: proximity to an important railway junction

items.action: Since the last war, trucks replaced rivercraft, whose traffic is now limited to the estuary; owners moved to the estuary, trade, farming or became truck drivers.
Land use around Lisbon followed a Von Thünen pattern shaped by transport cost: vegetables nearest, then quality wine, firewood, charcoal, then cheap wine and wheat along the Tagus.

numbers.what: distance from Lisbon for cheap wine and wheat zone

items.place: Lisbon hinterland; Tagus up to 100 km from Lisbon

items.action: Timber from distant regions reached Lisbon by coastal shipping from the western coast, or by log-floating on the Zêzere, rafts on the Tagus, then barges from the tidal limit.
Goods from the most distant regions, such as ashes, olive oil, meat and cheese, best bore transport costs.
Vintners' stores long stood on the south bank opposite Lisbon and in upstream harbours; some riverside industries and wholesalers later moved to northern Lisbon because of railway and haulage.
items.place: south bank of Tagus estuary opposite Lisbon

items.action: Saw-mills at Rio de Moinhos stand at an old timber-loading harbour for Lisbon; Praia do Ribatejo's are at the Tagus–Zêzere confluence where logs floated.
items.place: Rio de Moinhos (near Abrantes); Praia do Ribatejo

items.action: Cork industry was set up at Rossio de Abrantes and Chamusca, both river harbours whose main export was cork.
Rossio de Abrantes is a major wholesale grocery centre of the interior, a specialization owed to its harbour, which outlasted the railway.
items.conditions: harbour survived the arrival of the railway, now superseded by road transport

items.action: Before motor vehicles, clients, chiefly mule-drivers, came to the wholesaler at Rossio de Abrantes to buy goods.
Now the wholesaler travels to clients scattered over a north-south strip from Beira to the Alentejo, reversing the former distribution pattern.
The last chapter analyses location, site and morphology of Tagus harbours, including Rossio de Abrantes-Barreiras do Tejo, Constância-Praia do Ribatejo and Chamusca.
items.place: Rossio de Abrantes; Barreiras do Tejo; Constância; Praia do Ribatejo; Chamusca

items.action: Town plans of Tagus harbour towns show their life was shaped by their main activity; tertiary activities lay on riverside-parallel streets and squares.
Old civic and trade centres survived only in slumbering towns like Constância; in dynamic Rossio the old centre was deserted and activity moved near modern transport.

Plates show views of Constância, the Zêzere-Tejo confluence, Vila Nova da Barquinha, Tancos, Rossio de Abrantes buildings with ground-floor warehouses, and ruins near the old quay at Barreiras do Tejo.
items.place: Constância; Vila Nova da Barquinha; Tancos; Rossio de Abrantes; Barreiras do Tej
